TERRAFORM PLAN SECRET EXPOSURE CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Did your Terraform plan just print a secret in plaintext?

Paste or load a Terraform structured plan (terraform show -json) and get a deterministic report of every attribute value that looks like a real secret -- an AWS access key, a PEM private key, a JWT, or a URL with embedded credentials -- which the provider schema did not mark sensitive.

Nothing is uploaded. The file you load is read in this browser and never leaves your device.

1. Load your plan

2. What this plan would fail on

Resource / outputSidePathPatternValue (redacted)

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate before you apply?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — run it right after you generate the plan, before anything applies:

terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json
node cli.mjs check plan.json                    # human-readable, exit 1 if anything unmarked is found
node cli.mjs check plan.json --json

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the local file you name: no network call, ever.

What this checks — and what it cannot

Failure this is checked againstChecked here as

Sources and the exact scope: why a Terraform plan can print a secret even though the schema has a `sensitive` flag. Already run a general secret scanner like Gitleaks, or a broader policy scanner like Checkov? See how this checker differs from Gitleaks, this checker vs. Checkov, or this checker vs. reading the plan JSON by eye — the short version is they all catch different things. Config drifting from what a codebase actually reads is a related, separate failure — see Env Example Drift Check for `.env.example` rather than a Terraform plan. And the same plan file answers a second question this tool does not ask: Terraform Plan Blast Radius Check reports what the apply would destroy or replace — every replace on a database, disk, bucket or secret, with the attribute that forced it.

Common questions

Does this catch every possible secret leak in my Terraform plan?

No. It matches a fixed set of high-confidence secret shapes — AWS access keys, PEM private keys, JWTs, and URLs with embedded credentials — against every attribute value the provider schema did not already mark sensitive. It will not catch a secret in a shape it doesn't recognise, and it cannot see your provider's source to know whether a field should have been marked sensitive in the first place. Treat a clean report as one more gate passed, not a guarantee.

Is my plan uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses a pasted or locally loaded file entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only a local file — no network call, ever.

What file does it need?

The structured plan JSON from terraform show -json, not the human-readable terraform plan output and not the line-by-line terraform plan -json stream. Run: terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json

Why doesn't the report show the actual secret value?

Because the report itself is meant to be pasted into an issue, a Slack message, or a CI log — doing that with the real value would recreate the exact leak this tool exists to catch. It shows the first and last four characters and which pattern matched, enough to find and rotate the value without re-exposing it.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not security, legal, or compliance advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or your own provider's documentation. It matches a fixed set of known secret shapes against unmarked attribute values in the plan you supplied — it cannot prove the absence of a leak, only report the patterns it found. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for rotating any credential it flags. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The plan you load is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded, file_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checkov.html.text:
← Back to Terraform Plan Secret Exposure Check

This checker vs. Checkov

Checkov, an open-source project originally from Bridgecrew and now maintained under Palo Alto Networks' Prisma Cloud, is a broad static analysis engine for infrastructure as code. Out of the box it ships hundreds of built-in policies spanning Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests, Dockerfiles, Helm charts, and more -- public storage buckets, open security groups, missing encryption at rest, weak IAM policies, and dozens of other misconfiguration classes. A general-purpose secrets scanner is bundled in as one module among that much larger policy set. It is a Python package, installed with pip install checkov, and it can scan a Terraform structured plan JSON in addition to raw source.

This checker does one narrow thing and nothing else. It is a zero-dependency, zero-install browser page and a single Node file: it reads a Terraform structured plan (terraform show -json), reads the plan's own before_sensitive/after_sensitive markers first, and flags only the attribute values that look like a real secret -- an AWS access key, a PEM private key, a JWT, or a URL with an embedded username and password -- and which Terraform's own provider schema did not already mark sensitive. It has no policy database, no misconfiguration rules, no other IaC frameworks, and nothing to install: node cli.mjs check plan.json.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Catch misconfigurations across Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, or Dockerfiles -- public buckets, open security groups, missing encryption, weak IAM. Checkov -- that breadth is its core product.
Run one broad policy-as-code gate across an entire multi-framework IaC repository, with hundreds of rules to enable, suppress, or customise. Checkov.
Know specifically whether a Terraform plan's provider schema missed marking an attribute sensitive, so a real secret would print in plaintext into a CI log. This checker -- that is the one thing it checks, respecting Terraform's own sensitivity markers first so it does not re-flag a value Terraform already redacts.
Gate a deploy in CI on that one specific failure with zero installs, zero dependencies, and zero configuration. This checker -- node cli.mjs check plan.json exits non-zero on a finding, no pip install required.
Get broad, continuously updated policy coverage maintained by a vendor with a dedicated security research team. Checkov -- this checker maintains four fixed secret-shape patterns and nothing else.
Check a single plan file with no install, no Python environment, and nothing uploaded anywhere. This checker -- open the page, paste or load the file, done.

These compose rather than compete. A team already running Checkov for broad IaC policy coverage loses nothing by also wiring this narrower checker into the same pre-apply step -- it costs one dependency-free file and checks a distinction (respecting Terraform's own sensitivity markers) that a general-purpose secrets scanner is not built to reason about. And a team that finds Checkov's hundreds of policies more than it wants to configure just for the secrets question can reach for this instead, with no install at all. Neither replaces the other; they answer different questions at very different scopes.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Checkov?

They overlap on one narrow point and differ everywhere else. Checkov is a general-purpose static analysis engine: it ships hundreds of built-in policies covering misconfigurations across Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Dockerfiles, and more -- public buckets, open security groups, missing encryption -- and a general-purpose secrets scanner is one feature bundled inside that much larger policy set. This tool checks exactly one thing: does this Terraform structured plan contain a value that looks like a real secret (an AWS key, a PEM private key, a JWT, or a credential-embedded URL) which the provider schema did not already mark sensitive. If you want broad IaC policy coverage across multiple frameworks, reach for Checkov. If you want a zero-install, zero-dependency gate for one specific, narrow, high-confidence failure right before an apply, this is built for exactly that and nothing else.

Does Checkov already cover what this checks?

Checkov's secrets scanning is general-purpose pattern and entropy detection aimed at source files broadly, run as one module inside a much larger policy engine. This tool is narrower and more specific on purpose: it reads the structured plan's before_sensitive/after_sensitive markers first, so it only flags a value Terraform's own schema left unmarked -- a value Terraform already redacts is correctly ignored rather than re-flagged. That distinction is the whole point of this tool and is not what a general secrets scanner is built to reason about.

Why not just run Checkov instead of adding another tool?

Because they cost different amounts to adopt for this one job. Checkov is a Python package with its own install, update cadence, and hundreds of policies to configure or suppress if you only want the secrets angle. This tool is one dependency-free JavaScript file: node cli.mjs check plan.json, nothing to install, nothing to configure, exits non-zero on a finding. If a team already runs Checkov for its broader policy coverage, this does not replace it -- it is a much smaller, more specific gate for the one failure it was built to catch, worth adding regardless of what else runs in CI.

Is this page affiliated with Checkov, Bridgecrew, or Palo Alto Networks?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Checkov, Bridgecrew, or their parent company Palo Alto Networks, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. What Checkov currently scans and how it is licensed are described on its own project page and repository -- check there for what it covers today.

Only point either tool at a plan or repository you own or are authorised to test. That rule is unchanged by which one you pick.

← Back to the checker

No warranty. This is not security or compliance advice. It matches a fixed set of known secret shapes against unmarked attribute values in the plan you supplied -- it cannot prove the absence of a leak, only report the patterns it found. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

Everything on the checker runs client-side; nothing is uploaded. Support is optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-gitleaks.html.text:
← Back to Terraform Plan Secret Exposure Check

This checker vs. Gitleaks

Gitleaks is a widely used, general-purpose secret scanner: point it at a git repository (it can walk the full commit history via git log -p), a directory, a single file, or piped stdin, and it flags secret-shaped strings using configurable regex rules and entropy scoring, including inside archives (zip, tar, gzip) and encoded content (base64, hex, percent-encoding). It has no built-in parser for Terraform's plan format, so pointed at a terraform show -json file it scans the JSON the same way it would scan any other text file — by pattern and entropy, not by understanding the plan's own before_sensitive/after_sensitive structure.

This tool does the opposite trade: it reads only one file — your structured plan — and asks one narrow, schema-aware question per attribute: did Terraform's own provider schema already mark this sensitive, and if not, does the value match one of four fixed, high-confidence secret shapes (an AWS access key, a PEM private key, a JWT, or a URL with embedded credentials)? It is not a general secret scanner, does not read git history, and will not catch a secret committed in a variables file, a script, or a README — that is exactly the job Gitleaks and similar repository scanners are built for.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want my whole repository, including git history, scanned for anything that looks like a hardcoded secret — API keys committed by accident, tokens left in old commits, credentials in config files. Gitleaks — that is its core job, and it is built to run across a full checkout or history, not one plan file.
I want to know specifically whether Terraform's own sensitive flag missed an attribute on the plan about to be applied, without re-reading a config-wide scan's output to find the one relevant hit. This checker — it reads the plan's own sensitivity map and reports only the attributes Terraform itself did not already mark, against four fixed secret shapes.
I want a pre-apply CI gate with zero dependencies to install or a config file (.gitleaks.toml) to maintain. This checker — one Node file, no install, no rules to tune. (Gitleaks ships sensible defaults too; the difference here is there is nothing to configure at all.)
I want the report to redact the matched value so it is safe to paste into an issue or a CI annotation. This checker — every finding shows only the first and last four characters. Check your Gitleaks configuration and output format if you rely on it for the same guarantee; its default reporting is not built around that specific use case.
I want broad, mature, actively maintained secret detection across many source types (files, archives, stdin, CI logs piped in) with a large, configurable rule set. Gitleaks — it is the established, general-purpose tool for exactly that breadth.

The honest read is that these solve adjacent, not identical, problems, and a pipeline that both generates and applies Terraform plans has good reason to run both: Gitleaks over the repository in general, and this checker as the one gate that understands Terraform's own sensitive mechanism well enough to say precisely which attribute the schema forgot to flag, right before the plaintext value would otherwise print into the apply log. Neither replaces careful review of what a provider schema actually marks sensitive in the first place.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Gitleaks?

They catch different things and are not a substitute for each other. Gitleaks is a general-purpose secret scanner: point it at a git repository, a directory, a file, or stdin, and it looks for secret-shaped strings using regex rules and entropy scoring, including inside git history and archives. It has no built-in awareness of Terraform's own before_sensitive/after_sensitive plan structure, so run against a plan file it treats the JSON as plain text like any other file. This tool reads exactly one file — the structured plan from terraform show -json — and checks only the attribute values Terraform's own schema did not already mark sensitive, against four fixed high-confidence secret shapes. A CI pipeline that applies Terraform plans commonly wants both: Gitleaks for the repository and its history in general, this tool as a narrow pre-apply gate for the one failure mode neither a generic scanner nor a code reviewer can see — a provider schema that quietly forgot to flag an attribute as sensitive.

Does Gitleaks already catch a missing sensitive flag in a Terraform plan?

It can catch the resulting plaintext value if that value matches one of its configured detection rules or trips its entropy threshold — Gitleaks does not read or parse Terraform's plan format specially, so it is scanning the JSON as generic text, the same way it would scan any file. It has no concept of Terraform's own sensitive marking, so it cannot tell you specifically that the provider schema failed to flag an attribute — only that some string in the file looked secret-shaped (or, for a value that does not match its rules, nothing at all). This tool's whole job is that one narrower question: does the plan's own before_sensitive/after_sensitive map already exclude this value, and if not, does it match one of four fixed shapes.

Is this page affiliated with Gitleaks?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Gitleaks or its maintainers. Gitleaks is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, based on Gitleaks' own public description of its scanning scope.

See also why a Terraform plan can print a secret even though the schema has a sensitive flag, or open the checker itself to try it on a plan.

No warranty. This is not security or compliance advice, and this page's description of Gitleaks is based on its own public documentation rather than a determination about either tool's quality. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

Everything here runs client-side; nothing is uploaded. Support is optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-manually-reading-the-plan-json.html.text:
← Back to Terraform Plan Secret Exposure Check

This checker vs. reading the plan JSON by eye

The free way to look for a leaked secret in a Terraform plan is to open the structured JSON from terraform show -json and either read through it or grep it for known shapes -- grep -i akia plan.json, a search for BEGIN PRIVATE KEY, that kind of thing. That catches the literal string every time it is genuinely there and costs nothing to try.

This checker runs the same pattern match -- an AWS access key, a PEM private key, a JSON Web Token, or a URL with an embedded username and password -- but does one more thing first: for every match, it walks the plan's own before_sensitive/after_sensitive tree to the exact attribute path and checks whether Terraform's provider schema already marked that value sensitive, including the case where a whole subtree collapsed to a single true higher up. A value Terraform already redacts is skipped; a value the schema missed is reported. A plain grep has no way to make that distinction -- it treats every match the same.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Confirm a specific known string (a key you already suspect is in there) appears anywhere in the plan file. A manual grep -- that is exactly what it is good at.
Know whether a matched value is a real leak or one Terraform's schema already marks sensitive and redacts everywhere else. This checker -- it reads the sensitivity tree per attribute path before reporting anything, which a grep cannot do at all.
Catch a secret-shaped value nested several levels inside a resource block, next to fields that are correctly marked sensitive. This checker -- it walks every attribute path recursively rather than relying on a reader to notice the one field that differs from its neighbors.
Check an output value, which carries one sensitive flag for the whole value instead of a per-path tree. This checker -- it checks outputs with the correct, different rule automatically, instead of relying on a human to remember outputs work differently.
Gate a CI pipeline on this exact check with no install and no third-party upload. This checker's CLI -- node cli.mjs check plan.json exits non-zero on a finding, same as a grep in a pipeline, but without the false confidence of an unfiltered match.
Try it for free with a tool you already have on every machine. Manual grep -- no page load required, and it is a reasonable first pass before reaching for anything else.

A grep is not wrong, it is incomplete: it answers "does this string appear" and has no way to answer "does it appear somewhere Terraform already told you not to worry about." Every real finding a grep turns up is also a hit this checker would report -- the difference is what happens to the hits a grep cannot rule out, which on a plan with dozens of correctly-redacted attributes is most of them.

Common questions

Isn't grep -i akia plan.json good enough?

It finds the same literal string this checker's aws-access-key-id pattern finds. What it cannot do is the next step: for every match, look up whether that exact attribute path is covered by the plan's before_sensitive or after_sensitive tree, which collapses to a bare true at whatever level everything under it is marked sensitive. A human re-deriving that by hand has to open the sensitive tree, walk it to the matching path, and check whether an ancestor already collapsed to true -- for every hit, in a plan that can have hundreds of resources. Grep has no way to do that lookup at all, so every real match reads the same as a value Terraform already redacts.

What does a manual read-through of the plan JSON miss?

Two things this checker does that a read-through has no natural way to replicate. First, a nested block's secret-shaped field several levels deep, buried inside a resource that also has plenty of ordinary sensitive-marked fields nearby -- easy to assume the whole block is covered when only a sibling attribute actually is. Second, an output value: outputs carry a single sensitive flag for the whole value rather than a per-path tree, so a human has to remember that outputs are checked differently from resource attributes at all, not just check them the same way and get it wrong.

Why not just scroll through terraform show output before merging?

The human-readable terraform plan output already redacts anything the schema marked sensitive, which is exactly the problem: a value the schema forgot to mark prints in plain sight next to a dozen values that are correctly redacted, with nothing visually distinguishing the leak from the routine. Reading top to bottom trains you to trust the formatting instead of checking it. This checker reads the structured JSON, where sensitivity is a fact you can look up per attribute rather than a formatting choice you have to notice was never applied.

Is anything I paste into either process uploaded?

There is nothing to upload either way. Reading the JSON by eye or grepping it locally involves no third party at all, and this checker runs entirely in your browser against the file you paste or load -- or, from the CLI, reads only a file already on your own disk. Neither path sends the plan anywhere.

← Back to the checker

No warranty. This is not security or compliance advice. It matches a fixed set of known secret shapes against unmarked attribute values in the plan you supplied -- it cannot prove the absence of a leak, only report the patterns it found. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

This page names no specific product. "Reading the plan JSON by eye" and "grepping it" describe manual habits every Terraform user already has access to, not any company's product or service.

why-terraform-plan-json-leaks-secrets.ht.text:
← Back to Terraform Plan Secret Exposure Check

Why a Terraform plan can print a secret even though the schema has a sensitive flag

The mechanism

Terraform marks an attribute's value sensitive in two places: the provider's own schema (Sensitive: true on the field definition in the provider's Go source) and, for a value that flows in from a variable or another resource, propagated sensitivity through the graph. When either is set, terraform plan's human-readable output and the JSON from terraform show -json both replace the value with (sensitive value) or mark the corresponding path in before_sensitive/after_sensitive as true.

That only works if the schema author remembered to mark the field. It is a manual annotation on every attribute of every resource a provider exposes, and providers expose thousands of them. HashiCorp's own tracker carries recurring reports of exactly this gap: a provider adds a new attribute that can hold a credential -- a connection string, a generated password, a private key -- and it prints in plaintext until someone notices and files a fix (see, for example, hashicorp/terraform#16554, #26185, and #27577 for three separately-reported instances of this same shape of bug).

Where the plaintext value actually goes

A missed sensitive flag does not just affect the terminal running terraform apply interactively. The same value prints into:

  • Whatever CI log captured the plan step -- often readable by every contributor with repo access, sometimes public.
  • A pull-request comment, if a bot posts the plan output as a review comment.
  • A saved plan file (terraform show -json tfplan) committed by mistake, or attached to a support ticket when someone shares "the plan output" to debug an issue.

That is a much wider audience than the apply itself ever reaches, which is what makes a missed flag more consequential than the underlying credential simply existing in state (state has its own, separate handling and risks).

What this tool looks for, and why those four shapes

Rather than trying to guess which fields "look important", this checks every string value left in the plan (after Terraform's own sensitivity marks are respected) against four fixed, high-confidence patterns:

  • AWS access key ID -- the fixed AKIA/ASIA-style 20-character prefix format AWS itself uses.
  • PEM private key -- the standard -----BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY----- header used by RSA, EC, OpenSSH, and other key formats.
  • JSON Web Token -- the three base64url segments separated by dots that every JWT uses, regardless of issuer.
  • URL with embedded credentials -- a scheme://user:pass@host connection string, the shape a database or message-queue URL takes when the password is inlined rather than passed separately.

These were chosen over a generic "random-looking string" heuristic on purpose: a fixed format has an extremely low false-positive rate (an AMI ID, a hash, or a UUID does not coincidentally match an AWS key prefix), so a flag from this tool is worth acting on rather than something to learn to ignore. The cost is that a secret in a shape none of these four match will not be caught -- this is one gate, not a guarantee.

What this is not

This is not a Terraform state scanner, a secrets-manager audit, or a policy engine like Sentinel or OPA. It reads exactly one file -- the structured plan JSON you already have from your own terraform show -json -- and reports pattern matches against unmarked values in it. It makes no claim about your state file, your provider's source code, or whether a value it does not flag is actually safe.

Common questions

Why doesn't Terraform mark every secret-holding attribute sensitive automatically?

Because sensitivity is a manual annotation the provider's schema author adds to each attribute, not something Terraform can infer from a value's shape at plan time. Thousands of attributes across hundreds of providers means misses are a documented, recurring bug class rather than a rare edge case.

Does a missed sensitive flag only matter for an interactive terraform apply?

No. The same plaintext value prints into whatever CI log captured the plan step, a bot's pull-request comment, or a saved plan file shared to debug an issue — a much wider audience than the apply itself ever reaches.

Why check for only four secret shapes instead of any long random-looking string?

A fixed format — an AWS key prefix, a PEM header, a JWT's three dot-separated segments, a URL's embedded credentials — has an extremely low false-positive rate, so a flag is worth acting on. A generic random-string heuristic would flag AMI ids, hashes, and UUIDs constantly and teach people to ignore the report.

No warranty. This is not security or compliance advice. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

Everything here runs client-side; nothing is uploaded. Support is optional and never changes what the tool does.
